description.narrative: By December 2022, the Ministry of Labour of Qatar had supported joint committee elections in 72 establishments. To date, there are 72 joint committees at the enterprise level, with 578 elected worker representatives for more than 29,000 employees. The elections that take place at the enterprise level will form the basis for representative workers’ voice at the sectoral level, and, in due course, at the inter-sectoral and national level. The ILO designed guidance for joint committee elections and a training programme in five modules for joint committee members, covering their roles and responsibilities as per the Qatar Labour Law, employee participation rights (with support from the Government of The Netherlands), grievance handling and dispute resolution (with support from the ITC-ILO) and workplace inclusion. The training modules were based on relevant international labour standards. The ILO and MOL have continued to support the Secretariat of the Qatar Foundation’s central labour management consultation committee, including elections to the Women’s Subcommittee in February 2023. The ILO has provided training to the Women’s Subcommittee on roles and responsibilities as well as discrimination, violence and harrassment.

description.narrative: The Government has enhanced the dispute resolution process and access to justice, which directly relates to wage protection. There has been a high degree of compliance with the minimum wage since it was introduced, as evidenced by the Wage Protection System data, the research and the regular engagement with workers. However, the majority of complaints submitted to the MOL continue to be related to unpaid wages and benefits, including end of service benefits. While this continues to be a challenge and an ongoing priority for the MOL, a number of measures have been introduced that enhance wage protection. This includes stronger penalties for violations of the Wage Protection System; adapting the online complaints platform to allow for the submission of collective disputes; adopting enhanced procedures for conciliation; increasing the number of Dispute Settlement Committees from 3 to 5; and enacting measures to enhance the efficiency of the Workers’ Fund. As of August 2023, the amount paid from the Workers' Fund was approximately QAR 2.3 billion. Around half of this amount has been disbursed from the Fund to more than 70,000 workers. The other half was transmitted through the Fund from entities and companies to pay salaries and wages. The vast majority of payments coming from or through the Fund go to companies that have limited liquidity, the aim being to support the completion of the relevant projects or operations. The research on the impact of the minimum wage was commissioned by the ILO, and technical inputs were provided on the methodology, the design of the questionnaire, and the draft reports. The Survey was carried ou in May-June 2022. The ILO encouraged inclusion of low-wage women workers in the sample, as this has been a shortcoming of similar studies in the past. These findings were presented by the MOL to the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC) and the Global Union Federation) in a meeting organized by the ILO in October 2022. This data was presented by the research team to the Minimum Wage Commission. The MOL and the ITUC/GUFs have agreed that workers' voice should be included in the consultations around the review of the minimum wage from 2024.

description.narrative: The Ministry of Labour (MOL) has continued to operationalize the Occupational Safety and Health Policy adopted in 2020. Materials presenting the key DOs and DON’Ts related to the top five causes of work-related injuries in Qatar were widely distributed on worksites and on social media, and video animations on falls from heights and on road accidents, the top 2 causes of occupational injuries, were produced in multiple languages. Inspectors have carried out targeted inspection campaigns. MOL proceeded to a heat stress inspection campaign focused on construction worksites, the agricultural sector, delivery companies and the industrial sector. In July 2022, MOL decision was clarified that delivery riders are protected by the legislation and banned any delivery by motorbikes throughout the prohibited working hours. This campaign led to 463 worksites (almost all in construction) being shut down for non-compliance. To support the application of the heat stress legislation, MOL also disseminated communication materials for employers and for workers, which have received over 1 million views across various social media platforms, as well as guidance for employers. There has been a decline in the number of workers who visited the Qatar Red Crescent Clinics with heat-related disorders , which can be at least partly attributed to the prevention measures introduced in the new legislation, and the combined awareness raising and inspection campaigns by MOL. In May 2023, the Government of Qatar and the ILO held an international conference on occupational heat stress in Doha. The outcome of the event was raised awareness of the significance of occupational heat stress among senior officials, as well as the measures that can be taken to mitigate the risks – by employers and by workers. Extension communication efforts beyond conference participants was a key strategy to extend the reach. ILO provided technical assistance for the development and implementation of the annual inspection plan and targeted inspection and awareness raising campaigns on Heat Stress, Falls from heights, and accommodation standards. ILO has trained labour inpectors on Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) audit and risk assessment who were certified by the UK National Examination Board. ILO organized an International conference on Heat Stress organised in Doha with the participation of renowned scientists, researchers and tripartite partners. Qatar’s legislation, research, and campaigns on heat stress have also been shared by MOL and the ILO in several international meetings, including at the World Government Summit in Dubai in February 2023; at an online meeting on “Heat at Work” held by the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work in September 2023; at a regional meeting organized by IOM in Kuwait about the impact of climate change on migration and migrant workers in the region, in September 2023; and the MENA Climate Change Week in Riyadh in October 2023. ILO organized technical exchange visits to France and Sweden to acquire knowledge and expertise on all aspects of the planning and operation of the labour inspectorate (annual inspection plans, training systems, research, etc.)

description.narrative: The Ministry of Labour (MOL) has enhanced systems to ensure more timely and standardized services for migrant workers when applying to change jobs or in seeking redress for labour rights violations. These are the two top grievances that migrant workers have: challenges in changing employers freely, and the lengthy process of pursuing a labour complaint. The systems and services have introduced a number of changes in the past 2 years. The MOL has introduced several procedural changes to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of the process involved in changing jobs. For example, workers can check the status of their employment change application online or can cancel the application online. Further changes to the platform include an electronic version of the employment change form, providing reasons of rejection through SMS and waiving the notice period to fast track the employment change process. To ensure a consistent process of reviewing the employer change applications submitted by workers, the Ministry has adopted internal standard operating procedures. The linking of the electronic systems of MOL and Ministry of Interior ( MoI) can now prevent unscrupulous employers from taking retaliatory action after a worker applies to change jobs. MoI has introduced procedural changes and penalties to the absconding report system to address misuse of the system as a retaliatory action. The Government has also enhanced the dispute resolution process. Measures that have been introduced in the past 2 years include stronger penalties for violations of the Wage Protection System; adapting the online complaints platform to allow for the submission of collective disputes; adopting enhanced procedures for conciliation; increasing the number of Dispute Settlement Committees from 3 to 5; and enacting measures to enhance the efficiency of the Workers’ Fund. The ILO has worked closely with the MOL in identifying challenges that migrant workers face in changing jobs freely, or in getting access to justice. The ILO insights come from regular interactions with migrant workers, including receiving cases from workers directly, as well as various engagements with worker representatives, embassies and NGOs. The ILO proposed solutions with the Community Liaison Officers from the ITUC and the GUFs. Recommendations have been presented to the MOL in writing, as well as through regular exchanges with the Labour Relations Department and other relevant MOL units. Some recommendations are relatively easy to implement, e.g. adding a channel for collective disputes in the online complaints platform. Others require extensive capacity building, e.g. the ILO and ITC-Turin capacity building programme for MOL conciliators on mediation, that included the development of standard procedures for conciliation. The ILO has also helped to raise awareness amongst workers and employers on the legal provisions as well as the implementation procedures. Communication materials were developed in different languages for wider reach and dissemination. In addition, the awareness raising materials have been replicated and published by various media platforms and networks to ensure wider dissemination.
